prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to reach a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement advance that changes what can be observed. Magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler and recoil shifts while a large ensemble is interrogated, giving stabilities and uncertainties near 1e-18 that were out of reach a generation ago. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, relativistic geodesy, searches for variation of constants and the coming redefinition of the second all follow from it. The result is not one laboratory's claim: JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE routinely compare clocks and agree, which is the evidence of reproducibility I weight most. Credit is also unusually clean: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for driving the platform to record accuracy and stability and showing what it can do. Three of us placed it first independently, and I would add that it is a discovery of method, not an application.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is lineage. The optical frequency comb (2005) and the ion-clock and single-quantum-system work (2012) are already honoured, and part of Ye's contribution sits in laser stabilization and comb technology, so the prize could be read as incremental, or as an engineering refinement of frequency metrology. Other groups (Lemonde at SYRTE, Hollberg, NIST colleagues, and the ion-clock community) also made real contributions to lattice clocks, and the formal SI redefinition has not yet happened, so the societal payoff is still prospective. The committee could reasonably judge B012 or B009 to be a broader new scientific field and prefer them.

responses.point: Olsson ranked the lattice clock second and warned that the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes could make it an incremental step, and that the historical record on other lattice-clock contributors should be checked.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but think it is answerable. The 2005 prize honoured the comb as the ruler for optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped quantum systems. The lattice clock is neither: it solves the stability problem by interrogating about 1e3-1e5 atoms in a state where the trap does not shift the clock transition, and that is why the 1e-18 level and mm-scale redshift measurements became possible. Ye's comb-related work is the part I would keep out of the citation; the citation should rest on the magic-wavelength lattice and the clock performance it produced. I agree the contributions of Lemonde and others should be checked, but the two-name configuration still looks defensible.

responses.point: Pearce ranked the clocks sixth, calling them the most precise instruments ever built but questioning novelty relative to the 2005 prize, and saying the practical impact (redefinition of the second) is still pending.
responses.response: I agree that ranking should not rest on the pending redefinition; I would not defend the prize on that basis. My case is the physics: independent laboratories reach comparable uncertainties and compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, which is exactly the independent reproducibility you rate highly in your own instrument cases such as BeppoSAX and IceCube. As an instrument builder you will, I think, recognise that the magic-wavelength trick is a new idea and not just better engineering. Where we differ is whether the redefinition timing matters; I think the scientific maturity is already sufficient.

responses.point: Lindroth, who can judge atomic physics directly, put the clocks first and said agreement between independent laboratories is exceptional, with some uncertainty over lattice versus single-ion clock priority.
responses.response: I share your reading and would add a qualification on priority. Single-ion clocks (Al+, Yb+, Sr+) achieve comparable uncertainties, and a purist could argue they are the better standard. The lattice clock's distinct claim is statistical: many atoms give stability that single ions cannot match in practical averaging times. I would frame the citation around the lattice method so this priority question does not need to be resolved, and I would be glad to hear whether you consider that the right dividing line.

responses.point: Mehlig put optical-lattice quantum simulation third with Bloch, Cirac and Zoller and said omitting Greiner is a real allocation problem, with overlap against the separate Cirac-Zoller candidate.
responses.response: I agree the four-name problem for B012 is genuine and it is a main reason I put it second and not first. I proposed Zoller with Bloch and Greiner for that reason, and I do not think the allocation is stable enough to settle today: Cirac's claim is real, and Jaksch is not even in the credited list. The quantum simulation field is mature, but the prize would require a framing decision (proposal, Mott transition, or microscopy) that colleagues have not converged on, whereas the clock configuration is unusually clean. I would keep B012 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked twisted bilayer graphene first on the strength of a theory prediction followed by experiment, with robust reproduction though the pairing mechanism is still debated.
responses.response: The prediction-then-experiment structure is a strong argument and I do not dismiss it; B009 is my second alternative. My reservations are modest and I defer to you on the condensed-matter details: with the pairing mechanism unsettled, and sample-to-sample variability from twist-angle disorder still a practical issue, I would want to see whether the correlated-state phase diagram is as reproducible between groups as the clock comparisons are. If you can say that it is, my hesitation on maturity largely goes away, and the comparison would then come down to attribution of the experimental credit beyond one group.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Exact priority and credit for Lemonde, Hollberg and others, and for single-ion versus lattice clock arguments; I have not verified the detailed history.
How strongly B009 or B012 should outrank the clock if the committee prefers a broader scientific field to a measurement advance.
Whether a second part is needed or desirable, given a two-name credit for B049 leaves room for only one more person.
statement.conflict_note: A possible minor connection: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, the group associated with JILA, where Jun Ye works (and Ye is a credited name here). This was decades ago and I have no collaboration or financial tie to Ye or Katori that I know of, but the committee may want to note it. Separately, my WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, which matters for B040 and not for my preferred configuration. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
